extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers interested in Christian apologetics, social philosophy, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length apologetic essay arguing for accepting Christian orthodoxy as a coherent whole rather than extracting isolated moral truths; combines historical, empirical, psychological, and theological arguments. Useful as a model for reasoning about belief, evidence, institutions, and cultural effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthodoxy as guardian of liberty, innovation, and advance
rubrics_metrics.description: Orthodoxy is not only the safe guardian of morality or order, but 'the only logical guardian of liberty, innovation and advance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use doctrines (e.g., Original Sin, a transcendent God, the Trinity, a veritable crucified God) as instruments for social change and vigilance: 'If we wish to pull down the prosperous oppressor we cannot do it with the new doctrine of human perfectibility; we can do it with the old doctrine of Original Sin.' For awakening social zeal prefer doctrines that imply divine discontent (transcendence) rather than doctrines that imply contentment (Immanent God/Inner Light).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer fixed rules and clear dogmas to protect the poor
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed rules and clear dogmas are recommended as a means of protecting the poor: 'The RULES of a club are occasionally in favour of the poor member. The drift of a club is always in favour of the rich one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the aim is social justice or protection of vulnerable members, favor institutional rules and dogma rather than fluid, discretionary tendencies that benefit the already powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrines cannot be safely reduced to 'kernels' alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The objection 'take the truths and leave the doctrines' is answered by arguing that doctrines are not merely expendable shells: the living power of a faith depends on its doctrines and institutional continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware attempts to isolate a few 'comprehensible' moral truths while discarding the surrounding doctrines; the author asserts he prefers a coherent intellectual scheme and the 'living teacher' of the Church to isolated aphorisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence should be an accumulation of varied, converging facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief is grounded 'quite rationally upon the evidence' which, for the author, consists in 'an enormous accumulation of small but unanimous facts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to multiple diverse lines of testimony (one book, one battle, one landscape, one old friend) that converge on the same conclusion; diversity of kinds of facts increases their cumulative force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human exceptionalism as a legitimate datum for religious explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The startling divergence of man from other animals (capacity to make art, tools, civilization) is taken as a datum requiring explanation and pointing toward the supernatural: 'it is exactly where biology leaves off that all religion begins.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims about human nature, note the qualitative gap between humans and other animals—creative acts, civilization, cultural ornaments—and consider whether materialistic accounts suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical testing over sweeping generalisations about origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that religion 'arose in ignorance and fear' or that human sacrifice was once general are challenged: 'History says nothing; and legends all say that the earth was kinder in its earliest time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine primary historical/legendary records rather than repeating modern conjectures; do not assume primitive origins or uniform moral decline without checking the evidence in earliest sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions (priests, churches) should be judged by cultural and moral outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary to the charge that 'priests have blighted societies with bitterness and gloom,' empirical observation shows that countries influenced by priests often retain singing, dancing, coloured dresses, and open-air art: 'Catholic doctrine and discipline may be walls; but they are the walls of a playground.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate religious institutions by what they actually preserve or produce (arts, communal life, social resilience) rather than by caricature or selective anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept human testimony to supernatural events democratically
rubrics_metrics.description: The sensible course is 'to believe an old apple-woman when she bears testimony to a miracle, just as you believe an old apple-woman when she bears testimony to a murder.' Rejecting such testimony generally stems from anti-democratic prejudice or materialist dogma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing reports of spiritual phenomena, do not dismiss witnesses solely because of social class; a large body of consistent popular testimony deserves consideration and cannot be summarily excluded without circular reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not demand artificial 'scientific conditions' that exclude genuine phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Insisting on unnatural experimental conditions for spiritual phenomena is 'brainless pedantry'—if believers experience events under certain conditions, excluding those conditions guarantees failure of the test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tests that respect the authentic conditions under which phenomena are claimed to occur; analogies: ghosts prefer darkness as lovers prefer darkness—requiring bright sunlight is a category error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware circular reasoning in rejecting miracles
rubrics_metrics.description: Disbelievers often deny miracles because of an underlying doctrine against them, while believers accept miracles on evidential grounds: 'The believers in miracles accept them ... because they have evidence for them. The disbelievers in miracles deny them ... because they have a doctrine against them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot and avoid circularity: ensure one's denial of evidence is not simply driven by pre-existing theoretical commitments rather than engagement with the testimony itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: If faith is a condition for experiences, non-believers cannot fairly test them
rubrics_metrics.description: If miracles or visions require spiritual preparation or belief as a condition, then it is unreasonable to expect non-believers to reproduce them in testing: the critic 'has a most healthy right to laugh. But they have no right to judge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that some phenomena may be contingent on participant disposition; when investigating, account for participant-relevance rather than excluding it as illegitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of a living, continuing teacher/institution over dead exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church as a living teacher supplies ongoing instruction and surprise: 'The man who lives in contact with what he believes to be a living Church is a man always expecting to meet Plato and Shakespeare to-morrow at breakfast.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer frameworks or institutions capable of further revelation and teaching (living tradition) rather than treating great thinkers as static repositories of extractable moral aphorisms; living authority sustains expectation and continual discovery.
